Empirical Research Plan – Hospital Ownership & Public Medical Spending in California, 1986-1996
======================================================================

1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------
Preferred design: Staggered‐adoption Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with an event-study (Sun & Abraham 2021) specification.

Why it fits:
• The key variation is discrete ownership conversions that occur at different hospitals in different years (e.g., government→non-profit, non-profit→for-profit, etc.).  
• We observe the same hospitals before and after conversion; hospitals that do **not** convert (or convert later) provide natural counterfactual trends.  
• The “parallel trends” assumption is testable with pre-period event-time coefficients.  
• The DiD framework directly maps to the causal question: how does *switching* ownership type change the level (and growth) of public medical spending the hospital draws?

2. Treatment and Control
------------------------
Treatment variable  
 Treated_it = 1 if hospital i has ever converted to *for-profit* status and year t ≥ conversion year; 0 otherwise.

(We focus on non-profit→for-profit and government→for-profit switches because theory predicts the sharpest behavioural change. Other switch types can be analysed separately or pooled with interacted dummies.)

Treatment timing / event date  
 Conversion year = first year ownership_code_i,t == “FP” **and** ownership_code_i,t-1 ≠ “FP”.

Control group (counterfactual)  
• “Never-switchers”: hospitals that remain non-profit or government throughout 1986-1996.  
• “Not-yet-treated switchers”: hospitals that will convert in a future year but are still pre-conversion in year t.  
Both groups are included following best practice in staggered-DiD.

Unit of analysis: hospital-year.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------
A1. Parallel pre-trends – In the absence of conversion, treated and control hospitals would have evolved similarly in public spending.  
 Plausibility: same state regulatory environment; can be inspected via pre-event coefficients.

A2. No anticipatory behaviour – Hospitals do not alter public-payer billing **before** the official conversion year in anticipation of ownership change.  
 Plausibility: changes in billing systems/contracts often coincide with formal ownership transfer dates; we can trim (–1,0) window as sensitivity.

A3. Stable treatment and SUTVA – Once converted, a hospital remains in that status; one hospital’s conversion does not affect another’s public spending.  
 Plausibility: Ownership reversals are extremely rare; geographic spillovers possible but testable with county fixed effects.

A4. Exogeneity of conversion timing conditional on fixed effects and controls – Conditional on hospital and year FE plus observed covariates (local demand, payer mix), conversion year is as-good-as-random.  
 Plausibility: The 1990s California deregulation created external takeover pressure unrelated to contemporaneous public-spending trends; we will bolster with event-timing IV robustness (see below).

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
-----------------------------------------
T1. Selection on deteriorating (or improving) finances  
 If struggling hospitals are more likely to be bought by for-profit chains **and** struggle also drives public-payer spending, β̂ is biased.  
 Fix: include hospital-specific linear trends and lagged financial controls; conduct “placebo conversions” on hospitals that attempted but failed to sell.

T2. Concurrent policy shocks (e.g., Medi-Cal reimbursement changes)  
 If these shocks differentially hit rural/urban hospitals where conversions cluster, we confound β̂.  
 Fix: include county-year fixed effects or interact year FE with hospital peer-group indicators (urban/rural, teaching).

T3. Measurement error in conversion year  
 Mis-dating the switch attenuates estimates and violates no-anticipation.  
 Fix: cross-validate California OSHPD transaction files with AHA surveys; drop ambiguous cases; robustness trimming ±1 year.

5. R Code Outline
-----------------
```r
# 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)   # fast data work
library(fixest)       # DiD / event studies
library(did2s)        # Sun & Abraham helper
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ----
dt <- fread("ca_hospitals_1986_1996.csv")

# 2. Key variables ----
setorder(dt, hospital_id, year)

# Convert to factor
dt[, owner_type := factor(owner_type,
             levels = c("GOV", "NFP", "FP"))]

# Identify first year a hospital becomes FP
dt[, first_fp := ifelse(any(owner_type == "FP"), 
             min(year[owner_type == "FP"]), NA), by = hospital_id]

# Treatment dummy & event time
dt[, treat := (owner_type == "FP") & !is.na(first_fp)]
dt[, ever_treat := !is.na(first_fp)]
dt[, rel_year := ifelse(ever_treat, year - first_fp, NA)]  # 0 = first FP year

# Collapse other controls (example)
controls <- c("beds", "avg_case_mix", "teaching_hosp", "urban")

# 3. Main Sun & Abraham DiD ----
est_sa <- feols(log(pub_spend) ~ sunab(first_fp, year) + 
                beds + avg_case_mix |
                hospital_id + year,
                cluster = ~hospital_id, data = dt)

summary(est_sa)

# 4. Plot event study ----
iplot(est_sa, xlab = "Years relative to conversion",
      main = "Effect of FP Conversion on Public Spending")

# 5. Robustness: add hosp-specific trends ----
dt[, year_c := year - 1986]
est_trend <- feols(log(pub_spend) ~ sunab(first_fp, year) + beds + avg_case_mix +
                   i(hospital_id, year_c) |
                   hospital_id + year,
                   cluster = ~hospital_id, data = dt)
summary(est_trend)
```
Further robustness (not shown):  
• Re‐estimate on balanced panel (1988-1994).  
• Instrument conversion timing with county-level FP penetration interacted with post-1991 deregulation dummy (two-stage least squares with ivreg).

6. Expected Results
-------------------
Prediction: Switching to for-profit raises the amount of public‐payer spending **per hospital** by roughly 5–10 percent within three years. Mechanism: FP hospitals are more aggressive coders and less likely to cross-subsidize uncompensated care.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
------------------------------------------
C1: Credible control group / common support – 1  
C2: Parallel pre-trends verified visually & statistically – 1  
C3: No anticipation (pre-trend flat immediately before) – 0.5  
C4: No spillovers / interference – 0.5  
C5: Accurate timing & measurement of treatment – 1  

Total ≈ 4/5 ⇒ acceptable but must document remaining caveats.
